Forwarding Maya's procurement note. They need an explicit, customer-friendly explanation on session proration, rounding/minimums, and how discounts interact with billing granularity. High-level options below — please comment inline and flag any technical constraints (runtime/telemetry) or revenue impacts.

Option A — Per-token billing (simple, aligned to usage):
- Bill strictly by tokens consumed (prompt+completion).
- Minimum per request: 100 tokens (to cover metering overhead).
- Round up to 50-token increments above the 100-token minimum.
- Discounts apply on the per-token rate before rounding (discount reduces rate; rounding affects final invoice line items).
- Pros: simplest to explain. Cons: many very small calls still hit 100-token min.

Option B — Session-hour buckets (suitable for long transcripts):
- Customer purchases session-buckets (e.g., 1 session-hour = capacity to serve up to X tokens with persistent KV cache).
- Usage is metered to the second; partial session-hours are prorated to nearest minute.
- Small interactions within a session are billed against the bucket; if bucket exhausted, fall back to per-token billing for overflow.
- Discounts applied to bucket price for reserved commits.
- Pros: predictable for customers with long sessions; aligns to runtime optimizations (cache stays warm). Cons: billing complexity and edge cases for cross-session rehydrates.

Option C — Hybrid (recommended):
- Default: per-token billing with a 30-token per-request floor and 25-token rounding for basic tier.
- Offer an optional session-bucket plan for high-volume customers (>= 50k tokens/session) with proration by minute and a 1% add-on fee for cross-region rehydration.
- Discounts: apply to the list price of the chosen plan (per-token rate or session-bucket price) before rounding/minimums — clearly documented in contract examples.

Edge cases to call out:
- Cross-context within the same session: tokens are counted normally (we do not merge and then discount). Cache hits only reduce compute, but token billing is still per token consumed.
- Crossing session boundaries: if a single logical transcript spans two sessions, tokens are billed in the session where they are ingested; for practical purposes we treat these as separate requests.
- Aggregation of short calls: we currently do not auto-aggregate across independent requests unless the customer uses a batching API.

Revenue/ops note: rounding floors/minimums materially affect small-call-heavy customers. If they request a cap (e.g., per-call max rounding of 30 tokens) we should evaluate expected revenue delta.

Please reply with edits. I'll turn this into a one-pager + sample calculation for Maya.

—Neha

Thanks for the sample traffic. Attached is a short proposal and two worked examples (per-token and session-bucket). Below is the customer-facing summary we propose to include in the SOW / pricing exhibit. Please review — happy to adjust language.

Proposed summary (to include in SOW):
1) Base model: Per-token billing (prompt + completion). Tokens are metered at ingestion and billed per API call.
2) Minimums and rounding: For per-token billing we apply a 30-token per-request floor and round up to the nearest 25-token increment for the remainder. Examples:
   - A 14-token call will be billed as 30 tokens.
   - A 312-token call = 30-token floor + 282 tokens -> rounded up to nearest 25 -> billed tokens = 30 + 300 = 330 tokens.
3) Session-bucket option: Customers may elect to purchase session-hour buckets for long continuous transcripts. Partial session-hours are prorated to the nearest minute. Session buckets absorb short interactions without additional per-call minimums.
4) Discounts: Agreed discounts apply to the list unit prices (per-token price or session-bucket price) before rounding/minimums are applied. Invoice line items will show pre-discount list price, discount applied, then rounded billed tokens and the final charge.
5) Cross-context behavior: Tokens consumed across contexts in the same session are billed as consumed. Cache hits reduce compute cost but do not change token accounting. If a single logical transcript spans sessions, tokens are billed to the session in which those tokens were ingested.

Worked example (from your sample):
- Peak single-session transcript: 75,000 tokens. Per-token list price $0.0004/token.
   - Pre-discount charge = 75,000 * $0.0004 = $30.00
   - No rounding impact for large counts (rounding applies to per-request remainder only).
- Average session: 9,000 tokens -> pre-discount $3.60.
- If you choose session-hour buckets: example price 1 session-hour = $2.80 (covers up to 10k tokens effectively). Partial session-hours prorated per minute, so a 30-minute session uses 0.5 session-hours -> $1.40 pre-discount.
